title: The Ellington tribute TV show: the team and Jones's role as communicator
summary: Quincy Jones, Phil Moore, Luther Henderson and others assembled an all-star band for the Ellington tribute; Jones looked after Duke's musical interests.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Yeah. And it came off well, because we used it on the, 'Love You Madly,' TV show. That was another good team to work with, with Quincy Jones, Phil Moore, Luther Henderson, Marvin Hamlisch. I don't mean to just drop names, but --
That's interesting. No, it's important. This is all part of your career.
Oh, there was a team that worked on the
Carol Burnett Show that wrote a quartet for Sarah Vaughan, Peggy Lee and Aretha Franklin and -- I forget the fourth singer. It's a name.
Peggy Lee, Sarah Vaughan, Aretha Franklin -- Roberta Flack.
That's right. That's who it was. And they wrote a great quartet.
Yeah, I remember.
They wrote the wordage and Luther Henderson did the scoring part. And we all had different jobs to do. Phil had the -- he did, "In the Beginning God," with the James Cleveland Choir.
Uh-huh.

And Joe did quite a job on that. Then I did, "In the Beginning God," for Joe's personal thing, you know, so wherever he goes he can use it, you know. And that was a very -- I have to give Quincy a lot of credit on this. That Sunday, we were at A&M recording studios, you know, -- where Herb Alpert is.
Uh-huh.
And to see all the New York musicians and the California musicians together was quite a thing.
Yeah. They had like key people out of Duke's band and some alumni from of Duke's band brought in to work with the band that Quincy had here.
Well, let's see now. There was -- I remember we had Cooty Williams, Clarke Terry, Paul Gonzalez, --
Harry Carney.

Harry Carney. This is -- we're going back east, now. I'm trying to remember who the eastern (Unintelligible). And then most of -- a lot of the guys who were here had moved out here, still from back there.
Like Jerome, Jerome Richardson.
Jerome Richardson. Oh, like -- you could go down a whole list.
Yeah.
It was an all star setup.
It really was. It was a great, great band.
Yeah. And I was very proud to be a part of it even though my part was more administrative than writing.
Yeah, well Duke told me he wanted you over there to look out for his musical interests.

Yes, I know that. And I think Quincy realized that. We would meet at Bud Yorkin, and Norman Lear, you know, we would meet at the office and look at the small screen showings of Duke and whatever, and -- but that was before the rest of the writers came in. But my job was just to be a communicator.
Uh-huh.
Just to, you know, administrate and communicate. Which at that point I was so busy doing it I didn't know how important it was. But it was a big thing.
Yes, it was.
